newsitem.title: INDIA: Reunited Congress could tip India power equation.
newsitem.headline: Reunited Congress could tip India power equation.

text.p: The fall of former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao from his last party post could jolt a delicate balance of power in New Delhi as a more muscular Congress party closes ranks, analysts said on Friday.
A reunited Congress is expected to stake a greater claim to power and could pose an eventual threat to Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's 13-party United Front (UF) coalition, they said.
"UF Runs on Borrowed Time," read a headline in The Pioneer newspaper on Friday.
But Congress will take time to rally its forces and is not ready for fresh general elections, giving Deve Gowda some breathing room, they said.
"Congress will now like to have a bigger say in governance," analyst Ashis Nandy of the Centre for Study of Developing Societies.
"But Congress needs a few months to put its house in order. There is no consensus on a new leader, who will have to establish a power base," he said.
Rao was forced to step down on Thursday from his last Congress post as leader of the party's parliamentary bloc.
He had quit as party leader in September after a judge upheld a summons ordering him to appear in court to face criminal conspiracy charges.

But he clung tenaciously to the last post, which gave him influence because Deve Gowda's minority coalition depends on Congress to survive against the Hindu nationalist opposition in parliament. Congress has backed Deve Gowda without joining the government.

Pressure had mounted on Rao to quit after Congress suffered its worst ever defeat in general elections earlier this year. Bitter divisions had built up within Congress towards the end of Rao's five-year tenure, hobbling the party at the polls.

Ensnared in three corruption cases and surrounded by a growing number of critics, Rao bowed to the inevitable and stepped down, only minutes before a deadline that Congress party president Sitaram Kesri had set in an ultimatum.
Rao has denied any wrongdoing in the cases, each of which carry a maximum penalty of seven years in jail if convicted.
Several Congress veterans were jockeying for advantage before a vote set for next Monday to choose Rao's successor at the head of the Congress parliamentary party.

Hobbled by court cases and under fire in his own party, Rao had been in no position to lead a challenge against Deve Gowda. Now Congress, which controls at least 142 votes in the 545-member lower house, could flex its muscles, analysts said.
Congress trails the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party, which is the biggest single party in the lower house of parliament with 161 votes.

Deve Gowda's coalition has some 190 votes but they are split among 13 parties ranging from free traders to communists. Strains have emerged within the disparate coalition, especially over economic policy which is spearheaded by Finance Minister P. Chidambaram, whose liberal thrust riles the left.

Political analyst Rasheed Talib said Congress appeared split between two camps. One would be inclined to stake an aggressive claim to the prime minister's office. The other would prefer to share power with Deve Gowda by linking up with centrist parties in his coalition at the expense of the Left.
The prospect of a power-sharing arrangement helped to boost share prices on Friday. The Bombay Stock Exchange's benchmark index was up nearly two percent in early afternoon trade.

Financial markets are comfortable with Congress's liberal economic record under former finance minister Manmohan Singh. Some brokers hoped Singh would become Congress's parliamentary leader, but analysts said his prospects were thin.
"It is still early. Perhaps Congress will not pose a threat. When it comes to a crunch, Congress may back off because it may not be ready for elections," Talib said.

"The bottom line for Congress is how to bring down the regime without antagonising large segments of the United Front and provoking elections," Nandy said, adding that he did not foresee fresh elections before 1998.
